title: I analysed over 30k games on Steam and looked at the impact of AI disclosure on sales (again). I have some corrections to make on my work from last year and a new hypothesis about the impact of AI on Steam games.
author: randomstate42
selftext:
Back in December 2025 I compared over 9000 commercial Steam releases with and without AI disclosure and found that AI games received roughly 53% fewer reviews in their first month. That analysis went largely unnoticed until in the summer of 2026 PC Gamer and Dualshockers picked it up, then it exploded and ended up everywhere!

I haven’t touched the subject since then, mainly because it is so divisive and I wasn’t convinced I could contribute to the debate positively. But I’ve had more time to think and explore the data recently, so today I’m issuing an update.

A year on I have three times the data, a better model, and a new ability to see how AI is being used in each game and in my new analysis I revisit the question of just how impactful AI disclosure is on Steam sales.

You can read the full blog here: [https://www.game-oracle.com/blog/ai-update-2](https://www.game-oracle.com/blog/ai-update-2)

But in case you don’t the answer basically is, yes, the expected loss in sales is still there on the face of it; AI games receive significantly less sales. **But most of the damage is already done by launch day, before anyone has played the game, and that changes what the findings mean!**

Either the penalty of disclosing AI applies before launch and people refuse to support an AI game. Or, AI is the symptom of a wider problem, with people speed running development and not putting the care and attention into marketing and community building that a successful launch requires, and we all know that was a recipe for disaster long before AI was on the scene! (I establish this hypothesis by look at the time a store page is up prior to launch and the number of wishlists a game has prior to launch; AI games have both a shorter runway and less followers).

I urge you to read to the end of the article because there are many caveats and nuances to understand, but if you don’t, this is the main takeaway: approach AI with caution, if you do choose to use it then use it gracefully, but most of all give your game the run-up to launch it deserves.

comments.author: NikkiWebster
comments.body:
How do you control for game quality? 

I'd be interested to know what the percentage of positive reviews are on those games. 

Because it may simply be that, on average, games with AI disclosures simply aren't that good.

replies.author: randomstate42
replies.body:
Good question. You might be right but the honest answer is, I just don't know. The analysis can't tell "AI games are worse" apart from "players punish AI disclosure." Both would show up as the same signal.

If we look at the numbers alone: among games with 100+ reviews, the median AI-disclosing game is 82.0% positive against 87.1% for the rest. So yes, they're rated lower on average, but that doesn't answer your question tbh.

I deliberately don't adjust for that score. It's measured after release, and part of it is likely *caused* by AI use: either the game is genuinely worse, or players mark it down for the disclosure. If I controlled for it, I'd be asking "among games players liked equally, does AI matter?", which throws out the exact effect you're describing. It's also built from the same reviews I'm counting, and only games that already got plenty of reviews have a meaningful score. Adjusting for it would mean selecting on the outcome.

What I *should* control for is quality before launch: effort, skill, budget. Problem is nobody can measure that directly. I use proxies (prior releases, publisher backing, genre), and a sensitivity analysis shows how strong a hidden quality factor would need to be to explain the whole gap. Even then it's an observational estimate, so "AI games are, on average, lower-effort releases" remains a possible explanation for part of it.

replies.author: NikkiWebster
replies.body:
I realise it's difficult to measure things accurately when it's about the subjective enjoyment of random people.

But I think without factoring in price, genre, release date, etc. it's hard to really know. 

If you could filter for things like. 2D puzzle platformers at a $5 price point released in the same month. And then compare, but then you probably don't have statistically significant data. 

Or even removing outliers. Pull all games released in 12 months for under $10. Exclude games with less than 50% positive reviews, and then compare. 

I dunno, I just think it's hard to learn much without anything more specific.

replies.author: randomstate42
replies.body:
Fair, maybe the article buries too much of the detail and I should of summarised it better: a lot of what you're asking *is in there*

The model compares games of the same genre, released in the same month, on sale for the same number of days, with the same publisher status and developer experience. Your "2D puzzle platformers in the same month" idea is close to something I actually did. Our Steam Map groups games into a few hundred neighbourhoods of very similar games. Comparing AI games only with non-AI games from the same neighbourhood and release quarter changed almost nothing: 23% vs 12% reaching 1,000 sales, and AI games did worse in 107 of 111 neighbourhoods. I did this with 31,000 games, so sample size isn't the problem either.

Price I didn't control for and you're right to be skeptical. BUT AI games do lean cheaper (53% under $5 vs 47%). I left it out because price can be a *result* of using AI, since a cheaper-to-make game gets priced lower (that is an assumption tho). But a "same price band" check is a reasonable thing to run, so maybe I should do that.

Filtering out games below 50% positive I'd avoid, for the same reason as before. It throws away the AI games players disliked, and that's part of what we're trying to measure. It also drops every game that never got enough reviews to have a score, which is nearly a third of AI games.

The most specific thing I found is further down the post. Match games on how many followers they had *on launch day*, and the gap nearly disappears: from about 63% down to about 8%. AI games tend to launch with a store page up for 52 days instead of 167, and 6 followers instead of 20. Whether that's "rushed launches" or "players scrolling past the AI art before launch" is the open question.

replies.author: NikkiWebster
replies.body:
Yeah I think that is useful. 

My only thought with using sales numbers as the primary metric is that you can't really filter for marketing budget and marketing activity. I think the time from page creation to launch gives a small sense of this, but also without seeing what was done off-platform it's hard to extrapolate too much. 

Perhaps one thing worth filtering for would be what the positive reviews percentages would be if you remove negative reviews that gives AI use as a primary reason for the negative review. That would give a string indication if it can also be demonstrated that a certain amount of negative reviews causes Steam to show your game less. (Perhaps also account for games with no AI disclosure where reviews indicate a perception that AI was used).

comments.author: Kanalbanan
comments.body:
Interesting data. It’d be nice to investigate a couple of things further:

**Audience growth before launch:** Compare follower growth over equivalent periods to see whether AI games launch with smaller audiences simply because they spend less time marketing, or because they have a harder time attracting followers.

**Game quality vs. AI stigma:** The lower ratings are currently just a correlation. It would be interesting to see whether the difference is actually associated with AI disclosure or whether AI games are simply lower quality on average. One approach could be to use an LLM to assess game quality from Steam reviews, excluding comments about AI itself, and then compare games of similar estimated quality. It’d be a weak signal with potentially high error bars, but still. A signal.

comments.author: stolenyourgf
comments.body: Great follow-up, thanks for sharing the data. Could you split disclosures by how AI was used, e.g. "AI-generated then hand-edited/redrawn" vs. raw generated assets? I'd guess games where AI art was clearly reworked by hand (and say so) take less of a hit than ones where it's visible slop. Would love to see if the data backs that up.

replies.author: randomstate42
replies.body:
Good idea. The data can partly answer it. Our classifier already separates "used AI" from "says a person reworked the AI output" for each kind of use. I haven't modelled that split yet, but the plain numbers don't back up the idea that stating you rework by hand has any impact.   
  
Among AI games, the share that say the output was reworked by hand falls as sales rise:

* **Under 1,000 estimated sales:** 25% (of 8,185 games)
* **1,000 to 9,999:** 19% (of 719)
* **10,000 or more:** 13.5% (of 347)

This is not adjusted and I've literally put this together just now, so don't quote me on this! It might also just reflect who writes longer disclosures (or disclosures at all!)

If I was to guess, I would say small indie studios might be the ones keenest to say "we redrew it". It also measures what developers *say*, not how polished the art actually looks. I'll try a proper adjusted comparison for a follow-up.
